segments.text: If yesterday was about your body, today is often about your head.
Around now, the thoughts tend to get busy.
They say things that sound like you.
"Just one, and then back to it."
Two nights ago, on the evening of Day Xero, I said that if a thought like that showed up, you'd know what it was.
Today we make that a skill.
Here's a way to picture it.
You chose the route yourself, back when you wrote down your reasons.
A few of them lean forward and tell you, very confidently, that you're going the wrong way, and that there's a much better turn just here.
You could stop the bus and argue with them.
The trouble is, while you're arguing, you're not driving, and they have endless energy for it.
Push a thought away and it tends to come straight back, louder.
Or you could let them talk.
They're allowed to be on the bus.
They just don't get the wheel.
And we'll start with the body, because that's where a craving lives before it turns into words.
Take a breath, in a way that feels comfortable for you.
Bring to mind the last time you wanted one.
See if you can let that feeling be there, exactly as it is, without doing anything about it.
You're not trying to make it go away.
Notice that you can feel it, and still be sitting here.
What's the thought that comes with the feeling?
Whatever it says, try putting a few words in front of it.
You don't have to believe it or disbelieve it.
And your hands are still on the wheel.
A craving rises, peaks and passes, usually within minutes.
The thought that rides along with it passes too.
If some of the urge is still here, that's okay.
In a moment, you'll write down what your loudest passengers say, and one calm line to say back.
And today, when one of them pipes up, just name it.
Then carry on with whatever you were doing.
You're two days in, and you're the one driving.
